item.title: China welcomes more countries to explore pathways for AI capacity-building cooperation: spokesperson
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
China welcomes more countries to explore pathways for AI capacity-building cooperation: spokesperson BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- China welcomes more countries to join the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organization, explore more pathways for international cooperation on AI capacity-building, and promote global artificial intelligence (AI) development for good and for all with concrete actions, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said on Monday. Guo made the remarks at a regular news briefing when asked to comment on China's Progress Report on the AI Capacity-Building Action Plan for Good and for All, released at the 2026 Global Governance Forum (Xiongan), and China's views on the role of AI capacity-building in global governance. Guo said that AI is an emerging field in global governance, and a litmus test for the effectiveness of the global governance system. "The global governance system would not become more just and equitable without the collective capacity enhancement of the Global South, and requires concrete efforts to strengthen the representation and voice of developing countries," he said. Guo said China advocates for respecting the digital sovereignty of all countries. "We believe that every country has the right to possess the foundational capabilities for independent AI development, and to seek a development path suited to its national conditions and practical needs, one that enables AI to be applied in real-world scenarios, address real problems, and generate sustained value," Guo added. item.title: Displaced residents moving into prefab homes three days after Xizang quake
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
Displaced residents moving into prefab homes three days after Xizang quake A drone photo taken on Oct. 26, 2026 shows prefabricated houses at a resettlement site of a quake-hit village in Maru Township of Baqen County, Nagqu City, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Gaesang Namgyae) BAQEN, Xizang, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- Three days after the 7.0-magnitude earthquake damaged his home, Tsewang Khangshi was busy moving folding beds and quilts into his temporary new home. On Sunday, the 36-year-old villager from Baqen County moved from a tent to a prefabricated house, which rescue workers had rushed against the clock to build in the wake of the quake that struck on Oct. 22, killing 16 people and injuring 76 others. More than 12,000 residents were evacuated, and 339 homes and 20 livestock sheds were damaged or destroyed, according to local authorities. Baqen County in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, the epicenter of the earthquake, perches at an altitude of nearly 4,800 meters. Tiding over the cold winter has been a top concern for displaced residents like Tsewang Khangshi. Large quantities of disaster relief supplies had arrived in the disaster zone in batches. As of 11 a.m. on Oct. 24, 52,450 items or sets of disaster relief supplies had been sent to the quake zone, including 4,651 tents, 2,000 prefabricated houses, 11,772 folding beds, 5,715 quilts and other cold-weather necessities. Within five hours of the earthquake, the first tents had been erected. All affected residents, including Tsewang Khangshi's family, had moved into temporary tent shelters by Oct. 23. His family moved into a prefabricated house on Oct. 25. "We are so happy we can move into a prefabricated house," he said, packing quilts, clothes and folding beds into his vehicle -- all relief supplies delivered in the immediate aftermath of the quake. The high altitude, low temperatures and strong winds have posed challenges for both residents and rescue workers. Gusts reached up to 13 meters per second, making it difficult to keep warm, particularly at night. To provide better protection against the harsh weather, construction teams and power workers have worked around the clock to build sturdier, warmer temporary homes. The first 60 prefabricated housing units in the earthquake zone were completed at 2:10 a.m. on Oct. 25, and electricity was connected to the units by 8 p.m. on the same day. "We will ensure that affected residents have safe shelter, warm clothing and bedding, hot meals and clean drinking water," said Pan Zhiqing, Party chief of the Nagqu Municipal Emergency Management Bureau. "As more prefabricated units are completed, we will gradually move residents out of tents and into better-heated housing." As the new housing units became available, families began moving in, cleaning their rooms and arranging furniture. The sound of people carrying belongings and chatting filled the settlement in the afternoon sunshine. Outside, workers went from door to door, checking electrical wiring and the sealing of windows and doors against drafts. "All the prefabricated houses are fitted with chimneys for stove use, and we must ensure residents can stay warm through the winter," said Zhang Xuhui, a construction team leader with China Railway. item.title: China sees steady growth in domestic tourism over first 9 months of 2026
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
China sees steady growth in domestic tourism over first 9 months of 2026 BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- China's domestic tourism market posted solid growth in terms of both trips and travel spending from January to September this year, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism (MCT) said on Monday. More than 5.3 billion domestic trips were made during the first nine months of 2026, up 6.2 percent year on year, data from a survey of domestic travelers conducted by the ministry revealed. Urban residents accounted for over 4 billion trips, an increase of 6.6 percent from a year earlier, while rural residents made 1.27 billion trips, marking a 5.1-percent rise. Domestic tourism spending expanded 2.2 percent year on year to 4.95 trillion yuan (about 737 billion U.S. dollars) during these nine months. Of the total, urban residents spent 4.14 trillion yuan, up 2.2 percent, while rural residents spent 810 billion yuan, rising 2.1 percent. China aims to record 8.3 billion year-round domestic trips and 7.7 trillion yuan in year-round domestic travel spending by 2030, according to a five-year tourism development plan for the 2026-2030 period released by the MCT in July. In 2025, the country saw more than 6.5 billion domestic trips, with tourism expenditure reaching 6.3 trillion yuan, both setting new records. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. item.title: Together for greater progress in poverty reduction
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
Together for greater progress in poverty reduction Farmers harvest kiwifruit for domestic and international markets at a kiwifruit farm in Fengxin county, Yichun, east China's Jiangxi province. (Photo/Zhou Liang) Eradicating poverty has long been a shared aspiration of humanity and remains one of the most formidable challenges to global development. Learning from poverty reduction efforts, building international consensus, deepening practical multilateral cooperation, and advancing the global fight against poverty are shared missions and responsibilities of the international community. As the world's largest developing country, China struggled with poverty for a long time. To tackle this global challenge, China rolled out the poverty alleviation campaign unmatched in human history in scale, intensity, and number of people benefiting, achieving a remarkable milestone in human development. After eight years of sustained effort, China lifted nearly 100 million rural residents out of absolute poverty, achieving the poverty reduction target of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development 10 years ahead of schedule. Since the launch of reform and opening-up more than four decades ago, China has lifted over 800 million people out of poverty, accounting for more than 70 percent of the global total over the same period. Following the country's historic victory in the fight against poverty, China spent five years consolidating those gains and effectively linking poverty alleviation with rural revitalization. All related tasks were successfully completed, and the bottom line of preventing a large-scale relapse into poverty was firmly upheld. China's historic achievements in poverty reduction have contributed Chinese wisdom and solutions to the global cause. African scholars visit smart blueberry cultivation facilities and AI-powered crop management systems at a specialty agricultural park in Jinhua, east China's Zhejiang province. (Photo/Shi Bufa) Through years of exploration and practice, China has forged a path to poverty reduction with Chinese characteristics and developed its own theory of poverty alleviation, making significant original contributions to enriching the study of poverty eradication. Chinese President Xi Jinping's works, including "Up and Out of Poverty," have been translated into multiple languages and have become important reading for political leaders and scholars in many countries. China's sound approach to poverty reduction, effective institutional design, and targeted poverty alleviation efforts offer valuable ideas and practical pathways that can be learned from, replicated, and adapted by other countries seeking to help people still living in poverty achieve prosperity and well-being. United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has said that China's targeted poverty alleviation strategy is an important pathway toward achieving poverty reduction goals of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development, and that China's experience offers valuable lessons for developing countries. China has consistently been a committed advocate and practitioner in global poverty reduction and development. At its core, poverty reduction is a development issue. Over the years, China has provided development assistance to more than 160 countries. It has launched the Global Partnership for Poverty Alleviation and Development, and announced eight actions for global development. China has listed poverty reduction as the top priority among the eight areas of cooperation under the Global Development Initiative and included "promoting global cooperation in poverty reduction" in the draft outline of its 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030). In Cambodia, the project dubbed the Cambodia-China Friendship Village for Poverty Alleviation has helped improve local residents' quality of life. In Madagascar, Chinese agricultural experts have provided hands-on training in farming techniques, leading to a substantial increase in hybrid rice yields. The Juncao technology has taken root in more than 100 countries and regions, becoming a "grass of happiness" that benefits communities around the world. More than 1,000 mu (about 66.67 hectares) of saline-alkali land has been transformed into marine aquaculture ponds for raising swimming crabs and other seafood in Yinzhou district, Ningbo, east China's Zhejiang province. (Photo/Zheng Kaixia) China has consistently sought to turn its own development experience into international public goods that can be shared with the world. Through practical cooperation and stronger South-South cooperation, it continues to advance global efforts to tackle poverty and support countries in pursuing shared development. The world is now entering the final push to achieve the poverty reduction goals of the UN 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. Affected by a combination of factors, including sluggish economic growth, frequent geopolitical conflicts and the politicization of development issues, global poverty reduction has stalled, while deep-seated challenges, including imbalances in development between the Global North and the Global South and growing development deficits, have become increasingly pronounced. A recent report jointly released by the UN Development Programme and the Oxford Poverty and Human Development Initiative, University of Oxford, shows that 1.2 billion people worldwide still live in acute multidimensional poverty. In the face of these daunting challenges, the international community must stand together, share responsibility, learn from one another's development experiences and deepen practical cooperation. Only through such collective efforts can we build a more inclusive, equitable and resilient global development framework. A just cause finds great support, and a journey with many companions gets far. China will continue to work hand in hand with the international community, share its experience in poverty reduction and help more countries explore paths to poverty alleviation and sustainable development suited to their own national conditions. Together, we can build a better world free from poverty and blessed with shared prosperity. item.title: At China's Canton Fair, foreign buyers seek more than products
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
At China's Canton Fair, foreign buyers seek more than products A staff member of a motorcycle part company introduces the company's products to overseas buyers at the motorcycle section of the 140th China Import and Export Fair, Oct. 15. (Photo/Huang Jiming) The 140th China Import and Export Fair, also known as the Canton Fair, is underway in Guangzhou, south China's Guangdong province, attracting around 340,000 overseas buyers. Business negotiations remain brisk inside the exhibition halls, but many buyers are also taking their visits beyond the fairgrounds to factories across the Pearl River Delta. They are touring production lines, examining supply chains, and discussing joint R&D. More and more overseas buyers are coming to China not just to source products, but to find solutions -- a growing trend in China's trade and economic exchanges with the world. The shift from buying products to seeking solutions reflects a broader evolution in the value China's industries offer. In the past, international buyers often arrived in China with specific shopping lists. They compared prices, checked delivery schedules, and placed orders, with cooperation largely ending once a transaction was completed. Today, many overseas buyers come armed with technical blueprints and market hurdles: how to streamline the whole supply chain from product design to mass production; how to drive down costs quickly when rolling out new technologies; and how to shorten R&D lead times amid ever-shifting consumer trends. These questions are difficult for any single factory to answer on its own. China's comprehensive industrial system and well-developed supply chain networks, however, can provide end-to-end solutions. Overseas buyers who come to China to find partners gain more than a product supplier. They gain access to a complete industrial ecosystem encompassing raw material supplies, component manufacturing, technical services, and large-scale production. The shift from supplying products to coordinating across entire industrial chains shows how the competitiveness of Chinese manufacturing is increasingly extending across the value chain. Innovations in new energy vehicles, intelligent manufacturing, and industrial robotics span multiple fields, including mechanical engineering, electronic components, software systems, and materials processing. If any link fails to connect smoothly with the others, a promising technical concept may never make it to mass production. China's advantage lies in its ability to bring together the necessary supporting resources within a relatively compact industrial network, rapidly adjust designs in response to market feedback, and refine products through large-scale production. When overseas buyers visit factories in person, they are looking beyond the production capabilities of an individual company. They are also assessing how efficiently upstream and downstream businesses work together and how quickly the wider industrial ecosystem can respond to their needs. A humanoid robot showcases its boxing skills at the 140th China Import and Export Fair, Oct. 15. (Photo/Wang Meiyan) The shift from Chinese companies going global to overseas buyers coming to China reflects a change in direction, but the underlying principle remains the same: openness, cooperation, mutual benefit and win-win outcomes. This is more than a simple reversal of the flow of business. It reflects closer two-way engagement in international trade as industrial specialization deepens. By expanding overseas, Chinese companies can reach new markets and allocate resources globally. Overseas businesses, meanwhile, can tap into China's industrial support networks, technological capabilities and market scale to unlock new growth opportunities. Supply chains have never been isolated production lines exclusive to a single country. They are collaborative networks in which businesses across countries participate and work together. By complementing one another's strengths, they can create greater value together. At a time when global industrial and supply chains face multiple sources of uncertainty, businesses are placing greater emphasis than ever on supply chain stability, flexibility and resilience. For overseas buyers, a visit to a Chinese factory is therefore more than a sourcing trip. It is also a vote of confidence in China's industrial capabilities, business environment and development potential. Where traditional trade exhibitions once functioned primarily as transactional platforms, direct industrial engagement now cultivates enduring partnerships. A single facility tour can initiate a multi-year agreement; a joint production initiative can integrate enterprises across multiple regions. China's foreign trade is evolving not only in how businesses cooperate, but also in the role Chinese industries play in global commerce. By making better products, strengthening industrial chains and further improving the environment for opening up, China can help more businesses find partners, room for innovation and opportunities for growth. These connections are making the economic and trade ties between China and the rest of the world ever stronger. Overseas buyers discuss machinery specifications with a Chinese technician at the machinery and equipment exhibition zone of the 140th China Import and Export Fair, Oct. 19. (Photo/Wang Meiyan) Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: 9th CIIE set to see record number of product debuts
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
9th CIIE set to see record number of product debuts Flowers are in full bloom at the south square of the National Exhibition and Convention Center (Shanghai), venue for the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE), on Oct. 17, 2026. (Photo/Wang Yadong) The 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) will be held in Shanghai from Nov. 5 to 10. A total of 162 countries, regions, and international organizations are expected to participate, with the exhibition area exceeding 440,000 square meters for the first time. China's Vice Minister of Commerce Yan Dong said this year's CIIE will seek to become more market-oriented, distinctive, and professional, with three key highlights. A stronger commitment to openness. The Country Exhibition of the 9th CIIE will bring together 69 countries and international organizations, more than last year. Canada and Sri Lanka will serve as the guest countries of honor, while Moldova, Romania, and three other countries, along with the United Nations Development Programme, will participate for the first time. At the Business Exhibition of the 9th CIIE, U.S. companies will occupy more than 50,000 square meters of exhibition space, maintaining their top spot for the eighth consecutive year. Their exhibition area has grown by 1,500 square meters from last year. The Hongqiao International Economic Forum, held alongside the expo, will release a report on China's export capacity development for the first time. Stronger momentum for innovation. For the first time, the number of Fortune Global 500 companies and industry leaders participating in the expo will exceed 300. Nearly 200 companies and institutions that have participated in every previous edition will return to this year's expo, while more than 2,000 companies will make their debut. Photo shows the Bund in Shanghai. (Photo/Wang Gang) So far, more than 480 products have been confirmed for their global, Asian, or China debut at the expo, setting a new record. More opportunities for shared growth. Six international organizations, including the United Nations Conference on Trade and Development and the United Nations Industrial Development Organization, will participate in the expo. Government departments and local authorities will work together to organize more than 40 trade delegations and over 600 sub-delegations to the expo to explore business and procurement opportunities. The Business Exhibition of the 9th CIIE will exceed 370,000 square meters for the first time. A total of 4,142 companies from 148 countries and regions have signed up, the highest number in the expo's history. Xiao Lu, deputy Party secretary of the China International Import Expo Bureau, said the exhibition areas for medical equipment, healthcare products, consumer goods, and food and agricultural products have all been expanded. The Asia-Africa Products Zone will also be upgraded, with more space for African exhibitors. Free booth space for companies from least-developed countries will increase by 17 percent. More than 200 products making their global debut or first appearance at the expo will be showcased. They include a cochlear implant capable of detecting sound from all directions, a prototype 6G terminal and a water treatment system that can soften and remineralize water simultaneously. For the first time, the expo will feature a global consumer brands showcase. "Around 100 long-established, high-quality brands with strong consumer recognition have been selected, with a focus on the guest countries of honor and those featured in this year's 'Export to China' theme," said Xiao. The CIIE Shanghai Events and Conferences will provide exhibitors and business visitors with an efficient platform for communication and exchange. Nearly 100 events are being planned, including the release of research reports on companies expanding overseas and bulk commodity price indexes. New platforms and services will also be launched, including a cross-border data compliance platform and a digital credit insurance service on the China (Shanghai) International Trade Single Window, while facilitating the signing of a series of cooperation agreements. In the first eight months of this year, Shanghai's imports hit a record 1.87 trillion yuan (about $280 billion), accounting for 12.8 percent of China's total imports. As host city of the CIIE, Shanghai is exploring new ways to further expand imports. Customs officers inspect air-freighted exhibits arriving for the 9th China International Import Expo (CIIE) at Shanghai Pudong International Airport in Shanghai on Oct. 13, 2026. (Photo/Shen Chunchen) Lu Shan, vice mayor of Shanghai, said the city is working to speed up quarantine approval for imported goods and facilitate the transition of goods temporarily imported for exhibition into regular imports for domestic market. It is also upgrading the Waigaoqiao, Hongqiao and Huaihai Xintiandi National Import Trade Promotion and Innovation Demonstration Zones. On the supply-chain front, Shanghai is attracting and developing leading supply-chain companies to strengthen its global sourcing and distribution capabilities. The city has introduced 18 measures to facilitate customs clearance and set up 123 dedicated customs service desks and channels for the CIIE, enabling exhibits to be inspected and released upon arrival. The number of business negotiation areas has increased to 19, with a total area three times that of the previous edition. Lu said more exhibitors are shifting from participating in the six-day expo to establishing a long-term presence in China and increasing their investment. In the first eight months, the actual use of foreign capital in Shanghai reached $11.59 billion, up 6.9 percent year on year. The city is now home to 1,120 regional headquarters of multinational companies and 675 foreign-funded R&D centers. Leveraging the CIIE, Shanghai is advancing institutional innovation, strengthening financial support and improving business services to foster a world-class business environment that is market-oriented, law-based and aligned with international standards. The city has introduced streamlined inspection procedures for imported consumer goods making their debut in China. Customs clearance time has been reduced from a minimum of seven days to as little as same-day release, helping more than 30,000 new products make their Shanghai debut faster. Since 2018, Shanghai has attracted more than 1,700 high-profile stores making their debut in China, Asia or worldwide. Related Stories Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Explainer: How a ruling party rules itself -- CPC's perspective
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-27
Explainer: How a ruling party rules itself -- CPC's perspective This photo taken on March 11, 2026 shows the Great Hall of the People, the venue for the closing meeting of the fourth session of the 14th National Committee of the Chinese People's Political Consultative Conference (CPPCC), in Beijing, capital of China. (Xinhua/Wang Xi) BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- With more than 100 million members and the responsibility of governing a country of over 1.4 billion people, the Communist Party of China (CPC) faces an enduring task: identifying and addressing issues within its own ranks. The task has taken on fresh relevance as the CPC prepares to convene the fifth plenary session of its 20th Central Committee in Beijing on Monday. The four-day meeting is scheduled to deliberate on a draft decision on several major issues on persistently advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance. As Chinese President Xi Jinping, also general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, has pointed out, the CPC's full and rigorous self-governance is a great practice in the Party's self-reform in the new era, and has created a new frontier in its self-reform. WHY PERSISTENT SELF-REFORM? At a gathering marking the CPC's 105th founding anniversary in July, Xi said the Party focuses on self-strengthening and always brims with vigor and vitality, referring to it as one of its fine qualities with no parallel among other political parties and political forces. In its pursuit of a better life for the Chinese people, the Party has addressed development challenges through comprehensively deepening reform, while pursuing self-reform to enhance its governing capacity. Since the reform and opening-up in 1978, China has undergone profound transformations. Having achieved tremendous success from humble beginnings, reform efforts have now entered a "deep-water zone." Xi once compared the remaining difficult reforms as "tough bones that are hard to chew." As reforms have advanced into more complex stages, the CPC views full and rigorous governance of the Party as an essential guarantee. Under the banner of self-reform, the CPC has made persistent efforts to improve Party conduct, build a clean government and fight corruption. Haris Bilal Malik, a research fellow at the Institute of Strategic Studies Islamabad in Pakistan, said the CPC's approach treated self-reform as a continuing responsibility of the governing organization. Internal inspections, disciplinary supervision and anti-corruption measures were intended to identify organizational weaknesses, enforce standards of conduct and strengthen policy implementation, he said. Members of Communist Party of China (CPC) review the Party admission oath beside the replica of a boat, now referred to as the Red Boat, on which CPC founders concluded their meeting in 1921, on Nanhu Lake in Jiaxing, east China's Zhejiang Province, June 30, 2025. (Xinhua/Xu Yu) Helga Zepp-LaRouche, founder and president of the Schiller Institute, linked the CPC's concept of self-reform to the Confucian tradition of lifelong learning and self-improvement. She said improving governance capacity required a political culture within the Party that was oriented toward serving the people. Volker Tschapke, honorary president of Germany's Prussian Society, said the CPC's efforts went beyond short-term campaigns, reflecting a commitment to continuous self-examination. "This is not for show, this is character," he told Xinhua. HOW DOES OVERSIGHT BECOME ROUTINE? A central question is how self-reform efforts can bring about lasting changes in how officials and institutions operate. The central Party leadership's eight-point decision on improving work conduct, adopted in December 2012, set out rules governing research tours, meetings, documentation and other official duties. Its implementation has targeted problems ranging from the misuse of public funds for holiday gifts to misconduct outside working hours, with regulations, inspections and disciplinary measures reinforcing compliance. Anti-corruption efforts have also continued. China's top anti-graft authorities filed cases against 181 officials directly administered by the Organization Department of the Central Committee of the CPC in 2025, according to the work report of the fifth plenary session of the 20th Central Commission for Discipline Inspection. The work report also revealed that discipline inspection and supervisory authorities filed more than 1 million cases in 2025 and placed 47,000 individuals under detention. A total of 983,000 people received Party disciplinary or administrative punishment. Some 26,000 individuals voluntarily surrendered. Pavel Troshchinsky, a lead researcher at the Russian Academy of Sciences' Institute of China and Contemporary Asia, said China's anti-corruption efforts had moved from "paper requirements" to "real action." He highlighted the CPC's emphasis on ensuring that officials dare not, cannot and will not engage in corruption, combining punishment, institutional restraints and stronger ethical awareness. The CPC has also institutionalized regular inspections to assess whether Party organizations are implementing central decisions, exercising power properly and fulfilling their responsibilities. Inspection teams identify problems and provide feedback, while the organizations concerned must take corrective action under follow-up supervision. In 2025, the fifth and sixth rounds of inspections under the 20th CPC Central Committee were carried out in succession, completing full coverage of all provincial-level regions. The emphasis on corrective action can also be seen in China's environmental governance. Central environmental inspections examine whether local Party committees and governments are fulfilling their environmental protection responsibilities. Following the first round of inspections, which covered all 31 provincial-level regions by the end of 2017, inspection teams conducted a major follow-up review in 2018, covering 20 regions in two batches. Regulations issued in 2025 also provide for follow-up reviews of corrective action when necessary. In south China's Guangdong Province, inspectors found in 2018 that efforts to tackle pollution in the Lianjiang River had made insufficient progress. The findings prompted local authorities to accelerate wastewater treatment projects and tighten controls on industrial discharges. The river's water quality has since improved through sustained cleanup efforts. HOW DOES DISCIPLINE SHAPE DEVELOPMENT? A farmer shows an edible fungus cultivated with the Juncao technology at Yuanyi Village of Minning Town, Yongning County of Yinchuan, northwest China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region, Sept. 11, 2026. (Xinhua/Yang Zhisen) The effects of discipline and oversight extend beyond official conduct to the management of public resources and the implementation of development policies. Efforts to tackle corruption and misconduct in school meal programs offer an example. In 2025, disciplinary and supervisory authorities across China handled 61,000 cases involving corruption and misconduct in such programs, with 35,000 people receiving Party disciplinary or administrative sanctions, according to a report published in February 2026. The authorities also pushed for tighter oversight of school meal funds, procurement and food safety. Waleed Gaballah, a member of the Egyptian Association for Political Economy, Statistics and Legislation, said full and rigorous Party self-governance could strengthen fiscal discipline by curbing the misuse of public funds, reducing waste and improving the implementation of development projects. Emmanuel Matambo, research director of the Center for Africa-China Studies at the University of Johannesburg, said China's experience highlighted the importance of combining development commitments with the ability to recognize shortcomings and correct mistakes. Drawing on China's economic transformation and poverty reduction achievements, he emphasized that governing parties must ensure their policies deliver tangible benefits to the public. Tschapke drew on his visits to China to describe the changes he had witnessed in rural communities and infrastructure. "I have seen with my own eyes what has been achieved: how villages have blossomed through targeted poverty alleviation, how rural areas have found new hope, how high-speed rail connects people and hearts," he said. He associated those changes with the CPC's emphasis on public welfare and its efforts to ensure that resources reach the grassroots. Ruslan Yesin, head of the Department of Comprehensive Chinese Studies at Belarusian State University, attributed the CPC's governance achievements to its combination of long-term planning and pragmatic implementation, commitment to mutually beneficial international cooperation, and people-centered approach to development. Yesin said China's experience offers valuable lessons for the Global South in sustaining steady growth, improving livelihoods and enhancing the capacity for independent development. item.title: Xi leads CPC to advance full, rigorous self-governance
item.description:

Xi leads CPC to advance full, rigorous self-governance BEIJING, Oct. 26 (Xinhua) -- The Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee on Monday started a four-day plenary session in Beijing, which focuses on strengthening Party self-governance. This marks the latest move by the Party Central Committee with Xi Jinping at its core to strengthen the Party through full and rigorous self-governance. Xi, general secretary of the CPC Central Committee, has emphasized that exercising full and rigorous self-governance is an enduring task for the Party. "One has to be very strong if he wants to strike the iron," Xi said shortly after his election to the post of general secretary of the CPC Central Committee in November 2012. He later warned at a group study session of the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee that if corruption is allowed to grow unchecked, "it could spell the end of both the Party and the state." As China entered the new era, the CPC, the largest governing party in the world, faced unprecedented challenges in ensuring reform, development and stability, and addressing problems and risks confronting the nation. Xi has stressed that China's success hinges on the Party, and has made clear that the CPC must continuously strengthen itself through self-governance. In 2014, he explicitly put forward the concept of "exercising full and rigorous Party self-governance" as part of the Party's four-pronged governing strategy, alongside building a moderately prosperous society in all respects, deepening reform and advancing law-based governance. He has made full and rigorous Party self-governance a long-term strategy, as he considers it vital to the Party's long-term governance, the country's enduring stability, and the people's happiness and well-being. BREAK NEW GROUND In December 2012, Xi began strengthening Party self-governance by introducing a code of conduct that became known as the "eight-point rules." It established regulations for Party leaders regarding research tours, meetings, documentation, and other official duties, cracking down on lavish banquets, red carpet events, pomp, entourages, unnecessary meetings, and luxury perks that had once been regarded by some as typical symbols of power. Its implementation has helped curb longstanding malpractices, with effects extending beyond Party and government offices to wider society. "The eight-point rules have indeed brought about fundamental changes over the years," Xi said last year, when the Party launched a campaign to reinforce this code of conduct and consolidate the improvements it had brought about. Xi also launched an unprecedented anti-corruption storm that has swept every corner of public office, netting both high-ranking "tigers" and lower-level "flies." Some of the most senior officials -- including former members of the Political Bureau and its Standing Committee, top military brass, and retirees who left their leading positions years ago -- have been brought to justice. The anti-corruption campaign has continued unabated, with Xi stressing that the fight is an ongoing endeavor. In 2025 alone, 115 officials at ministerial level or above were placed under investigation, while 627,000 people were disciplined in cases involving misconduct and corruption that affect the people's immediate interests. The same year, China also opened investigations into more than 500 cases of cross-border corruption. At a plenary session of the CPC's top disciplinary body early this year, Xi again warned that corruption remains a problem that arises all too easily and frequently. "We must see the fight against corruption through to the end, no matter how great the resistance or how high the cost," he said. "No one who engages in corruption will be shown leniency, regardless of who they are, how high their rank or how great their contributions." EFFECTIVE APPROACHES To strengthen full and rigorous Party self-governance, it is imperative to uphold the Party's overall leadership. Over the past 14 years, the Party's leadership has been further affirmed in both the Party Constitution and the country's Constitution. Central commissions have been established to oversee key areas including reform, national security, cyberspace affairs, and financial and economic affairs. Working mechanisms for central decision-making and coordinating bodies have also been strengthened. Strengthening theoretical education is another approach. With Xi at the helm, the CPC has launched nine Party-wide major education campaigns. The latest one, launched in February this year, prodded Party members to fix their mindset regarding governance performance, aiming to stamp out the tendency among some officials to sacrifice public well-being in seeking to polish their performance records. This campaign built on the gains of previous ones on Party discipline and implementing the eight-point rules, among others, to advance the Party's self-governance. These efforts have gone hand in hand with institution-building. Under Xi's watch, the Party and state oversight systems have been improved. The National Commission of Supervision and local supervisory commissions were established to bring everyone in public office, regardless of Party membership, under supervision. And Xi has made discipline inspections a key instrument of intra-Party oversight. The inspection system allows higher-level Party authorities to send teams to examine how officials exercise power and carry out the central leadership's policies. Inspectors interview officials and members of the public, review documents and receive complaints. They report their findings to Party authorities. After each round of inspections launched by the Party Central Committee, Xi reviewed the reports in detail, assessed the problems uncovered and pushed for further improvements in inspection work. Since 2012, the Party has also formulated or revised an unprecedented number of internal regulations, building a comprehensive framework of rules to confine power in "a cage of institutions." Noting the progress, Xi also warned that in some localities, rules were poorly enforced while "hidden rules" prevailed. He stressed that regulations must become "high-voltage lines" and that power must be exercised transparently, leaving no room for such hidden rules. All these mechanisms are part of the integrated efforts to ensure officials, in Xi's words, "do not have the audacity, opportunity, or desire to become corrupt." LEADING MODERNIZATION DRIVE Full and rigorous Party self-governance serves a broader purpose: strengthening the Party's capacity to lead China's modernization drive. "To successfully achieve the goals and tasks of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030), it is imperative to focus on enhancing the ability and competence of the Party in leading economic and social development," Xi told senior provincial- and ministerial-level officials attending a study session at the Party School of the CPC Central Committee earlier this year. He urged Party officials to become more capable of pursuing high-quality development, serving the people, and guarding against and defusing risks. China has entered a critical period for achieving the goal of basically realizing modernization by 2035, and still faces rising uncertainty abroad and mounting challenges at home. At such critical junctures, strong Party leadership is vital to chart the course.
